flashcards.q: Name Cosmos DB's five consistency levels, strongest to weakest.
flashcards.a: Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session, Consistent Prefix, Eventual.

flashcards.q: What's the RU cost difference between Strong/Bounded Staleness and Session/Consistent Prefix/Eventual reads?
flashcards.a: Strong and Bounded Staleness reads cost 2x the RUs because they require a quorum read from two replicas; Session, Consistent Prefix, and Eventual read from a single replica at 1x RU cost.

flashcards.q: Which Cosmos DB consistency level is the default, and what guarantee does it give?
flashcards.a: Session is the default -- within a continuous client session it guarantees read-your-own-writes and monotonic reads at 1x RU cost. Outside that session (lost token, new client), guarantees drop toward eventual.

flashcards.q: State the hard logical partition size limit and why it can't be resolved by adding throughput.
flashcards.a: 20 GB, hard cap, no override. All items sharing one partition key value must live in a single physical partition for consistent lookups, so a logical partition can never be split the way physical partitions auto-split across new key values.

flashcards.q: State the physical partition limits in Cosmos DB.
flashcards.a: 10,000 RU/s and 50 GB storage per physical partition. Cosmos DB auto-splits physical partitions as aggregate data/throughput grows across many partition key values.

flashcards.q: List Blob Storage's access tiers and their retention/pricing pattern.
flashcards.a: Hot (frequent, no min retention, highest per-GB, lowest per-txn), Cool (30-day min retention), Cold (~64% cheaper capacity than Cool), Archive (offline, hours to rehydrate, cheapest storage), plus Premium (SSD, high transaction rate).

flashcards.q: Which redundancy configurations support the Archive tier, and which don't?
flashcards.a: Archive is supported on LRS, GRS, and RA-GRS. It is NOT supported on ZRS, GZRS, or RA-GZRS -- zone-redundant configurations cannot use the Archive tier.

flashcards.q: Compare Queue Storage and Service Bus on message size, ordering, and dead-lettering.
flashcards.a: Queue Storage: 64KB max message, no FIFO guarantee, no built-in DLQ (~SQS Standard). Service Bus: 256KB standard, up to 100MB via AMQP on Premium only (still 1MB over HTTP/SBMP even on Premium), FIFO via sessions, built-in dead-letter queue (~SQS+SNS combined).

flashcards.q: Contrast Azure SQL Hyperscale and Business Critical architecturally.
flashcards.a: Hyperscale separates compute from a distributed remote storage layer (page servers), up to 128TB, near-instant snapshot backups. Business Critical uses local SSD-backed synchronous replicas for lowest write latency but caps storage far lower (roughly 4-16TB depending on hardware generation).

flashcards.q: What is Microsoft's current recommended PostgreSQL deployment on Azure, and what's deprecated?
flashcards.a: Flexible Server is the recommended default for all new (and existing) PostgreSQL workloads. Single Server is deprecated -- lacks VNet integration and has a weaker HA story.

flashcards.q: How does PostgreSQL Flexible Server pricing compare to Azure SQL, and what's the horizontal-scale option?
flashcards.a: Roughly 40-45% cheaper than Azure SQL at equivalent vCore count. For horizontal scale beyond one instance, Hyperscale (Citus) shards across worker nodes via a distribution column, requiring real schema/query redesign for collocated joins.

flashcards.q: How does Cosmos DB's consistency model differ from DynamoDB's, and why does this trip AWS engineers?
flashcards.a: DynamoDB offers a binary per-request toggle (eventual vs strong) with no cost difference. Cosmos DB offers five distinct, per-request-overridable levels, two of which (Strong, Bounded Staleness) carry a real 2x RU cost -- AWS engineers often assume a simple two-way toggle and miss the three intermediate levels and the cost structure.
